title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
corePattern: Backtracking / DFS Enumeration of Cartesian Product
interviewTips: Ask to confirm constraints: digits length 0-4, only digits 2-9 (no 0/1), and whether order of output matters - any order is accepted.

Trade-off: iterative BFS expansion vs recursive DFS backtracking have same O(4^n * n) time, but DFS uses O(n) recursion stack and mutable path (more memory efficient), while iterative avoids recursion depth concerns and is easier to write iteratively.
Edge-case tip: explicitly handle empty input returning [] not [""]; remember digits 7 and 9 map to 4 letters, others to 3, so worst case is 4^n combinations.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force Iterative Expansion
approaches.intuition: Start with one empty prefix and expand it digit by digit. For each new digit, take every existing partial combination and append each possible letter for that digit, forming a new list. This directly builds the Cartesian product level by level like BFS.
approaches.theory: This is breadth-first construction of the answer space. Let res hold all combinations for prefix digits[0:i]. Initially res=[""]. For digit d=digits[i] with letters L(d), new_res = {p+c | p in res, c in L(d)}. After processing all n digits, res contains all n-length combinations. Correctness follows by induction on i. No recursion is needed.

timeComplexity.explanation: Let n=len(digits). At most 4^n combinations (3^n if no 7/9). Each combination of length n costs O(n) to copy when building strings. Total work is sum over levels, dominated by final level O(n * 4^n).

spaceComplexity.explanation: Output holds 4^n strings of length n. Auxiliary space is O(n * 4^n) for intermediate lists (can be 2x output at last iteration) plus O(1) extra besides output. No recursion stack.

edgeCases: Max length n=4 with all 7/9 -> 256 combos, string copying cost visible

approaches.name: Approach 2: Optimal Backtracking DFS
approaches.intuition: Think of building answers character by character as a decision tree: at position i you must pick one of 3-4 letters for digits[i]. Do depth-first search, maintain a mutable path, recurse to i+1, then undo (backtrack) to try next letter. When path length equals n, you found one complete combination.
approaches.theory: Backtracking enumerates all root-to-leaf paths in an n-ary decision tree where depth=n and branching factor=|L(digits[i])|. Invariant: path[0:i] is a valid prefix for digits[0:i]. Base case i==n emits a copy of path. Recursive step tries all c in L(digits[i]). Each leaf is visited exactly once, so all and only valid combinations are generated. Using a mutable buffer with push/pop avoids O(n^2) string copying per level.

timeComplexity.explanation: Same enumeration bound: up to 4^n leaves, each leaf requires O(n) to copy path to output. Internal nodes total is O(4^n) as geometric series. Cannot do better as output size itself is that large.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Output space O(n * 4^n). Auxiliary space is O(n) for recursion stack depth plus mutable path buffer of length n. This is optimal extra space vs iterative which holds two levels.

steps: backtrack(1) path=[a]: try 'd' -> path=[a,d] -> leaf "ad", backtrack; try 'e' -> "ae"; try 'f' -> "af"

edgeCases: Empty digits -> [] early return, avoids emitting empty combination
n=1: recursion depth 1, directly returns letters
All digits 7/9: branching 4, test stack depth n<=4 safe
Reuse of Solution object in Java: use instance fields carefully or make them local to avoid leftover state across calls
